C001035.text:
The President’s Budget Request is just that, a request. To compensate for years of underfunding, the Administration proposes to increase defense funding significantly and recognizes the annual appropriations process as the best way to provide additional funds. The request for just one DDG-51, the workhorse of the U.S. Navy, is insufficient to counter the ever-growing Chinese fleet, which now exceeds the size of the American Navy, as well as other global threats.  
 
While there are some improvements over last year’s domestic discretionary budget request, including full support for the Pell Grant program, the request has several shortcomings. For example, the proposal includes unwarranted funding cuts in biomedical research.  It would also terminate worthwhile programs like LIHEAP, which helps low-income families and seniors to pay their energy bills during the cold winter and hot summer months, and TRIO, which assists low-income, first-generation students in pursuing higher education.  Job Corps, which helps students from troubled backgrounds gain the skills and education they need to enter the workforce, join the military, or pursue higher education, would also be phased out.  These are proven programs that I strongly support.
 
Another program that is important to rural America’s economy is the Essential Air Service program.  The Administration is proposing deep cuts in the EAS program.    
 
After careful review, Congress decisively rejected these particular cuts last year.
 
While the Administration proposes a budget, Congress holds the power of the purse. The Senate Appropriations Committee will now hold hearings with cabinet members and agency heads to review these recommendations and to explore other fiscally responsible proposals.  I hope my colleagues on the other side of the aisle, who too often worked over the last year to impede the appropriations process and shut down federal agencies, will abandon their harmful tactics and work with us to govern responsibly.

During Women's History Month, I would like to recognize a leader and humanitarian from Southwest Georgia, Lillian Gordy Carter.

Born in Richland, Georgia, in 1898, she quickly gained recognition in her community for her diligent work as a nurse.

"Miss Lillian", as she was known, served in her local hospital, challenged the bigoted color barriers of the time, and raised four children with her husband James Earl Carter.

She played an active role in her son Jimmy's senate, governor, and presidential campaigns, where she gained nationwide recognition for her earnestness and Southern charm. G000546.text:
When I first ran for State Representative back in 1992, my aspiration was to represent my hometown of Tarkio, Missouri. I was a twenty-seven year old farmer who just wanted to stand up for a way of life and his community.  I never could have imagined where that decision would take me.   

For 8 years in the Missouri House and Senate, I fought for Northwest Missourians. From deregulating vehicle inspections, to standing for chain gangs, to securing funding for rural schools in the desegregation fight, I never lost sight of why I was sent to Jefferson City. Then, in 2000, the good, hardworking people of Missouri’s Sixth District entrusted me to be their voice in Congress.    

For 26 years, I have had the privilege of serving, culminating in becoming the Chairman of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and passing some of the most significant legislation in our nation’s history.  The responsibility entrusted to me is not something I have ever taken for granted. Not for a single day.   

What I’m most proud of is the work my team did when Washington made life harder for the people of Missouri’s Sixth. Together, we stood with hundreds of thousands of Missourians in their toughest moments.  We helped them cut through red tape and navigate a system that often felt stacked against them.  We got them answers and fought to deliver real results when they needed them most.   

I’ve said all of that to say this: After considerable reflection, 2026 will be my final year in Congress.  This wasn’t an easy decision, but it’s the right one. I believe in making room for the next generation. It’s time to pass the torch and allow a new guard of conservative leaders to step forward and chart a path forward for Missourians.    

That doesn’t mean I’m slowing down, not even close.  As I enter the 4th quarter of my life, I have more left in me. As many of you know, I don't let grass grow under my feet. We’ve still got a lot of work to do. I’m going to fight to protect Missouri interests as we work to shape this year’s Highway Bill. I plan to finish this last term the same way I started, full speed ahead.   

Maintaining our strong democratic republic will always depend on good people stepping up to serve from every corner of our great nation. I’m grateful for my colleagues in both parties, for the people I’ve worked alongside, and even for the opponents who challenged me and made me better. Public service isn’t easy. It takes hard work, humility, a thick skin, and a willingness to fight for what’s right.   

At the end of the day, I’m still the farmer from Northwest Missouri. You’ll find me back home on the farm nearly every weekend, after all, it is planting season. In fact, I’ll probably be on a tractor this weekend. And come Monday, I’ll be heading back through Kansas City on my way to D.C. to keep doing the job you sent me there to do.   From the bottom of my heart, thank you.    

It has been the honor of a lifetime.

.@GlyphosateGirl says it best: Giving corporate interests a liability shield, especially when their products make people sick, is completely un-American.

RT by @chelliepingree: 🚨 FARM BILL POWER GRAB

The 2026 Farm Bill quietly slipped in three sections that could shield pesticide companies from lawsuits, block states from regulating chemicals, and weaken water protections nationwide.

Rep. Chellie Pingree just introduced an amendment to delete them entirely.

Here’s the plain-English breakdown everyone should understand 👇

1. Lawsuit Shield for Pesticide Companies (Section 10205)

If this stays in the bill, chemical companies could avoid liability even if new evidence shows their product causes cancer or neurological damage. As long as the pesticide followed the label approved under Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), victims may lose the ability to sue.

Why this matters:

Bayer has already paid about $11 billion to settle lawsuits over the herbicide Glyphosate linked to non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma. More than 165,000 claims have been filed against Bayer tied to the product Roundup herbicide.

If Section 10205 passes, future cases like those could be blocked.

Pingree’s amendment removes that shield.

2. States Lose Power Over Pesticide Rules (Section 10206)

Right now states and local governments can create stricter pesticide protections than the federal government.

That includes things like bans on spraying near schools or buffer zones around homes and waterways.

Section 10206 would override those rules nationwide.

That reverses precedent set by the Supreme Court case
Wisconsin Public Intervenor v. Mortier, which affirmed that local governments can regulate pesticides.

Seven states currently allow local pesticide control.
Those protections could disappear overnight.

3. Weakened Water & Wildlife Protections (Section 10207)

This provision would exempt pesticides from additional review under major environmental laws including the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act.

In practice that means pesticides approved by EPA could enter rivers, streams, and habitats without additional permits or environmental review.

Government monitoring has already detected pesticide residues in most U.S. waterways, raising concerns about runoff impacts on fish, wildlife, and drinking water.

Why This Fight Is Exploding

Critics argue the provisions protect chemical manufacturers, override state authority, and weaken environmental oversight.

Supporters claim the sections reduce litigation risk, simplify national pesticide regulation, and protect agricultural production.

Pingree’s amendment simply removes the three sections entirely, restoring the existing regulatory framework.

What Happens Next

The bill is still in markup inside the House Agriculture Committee.

That means these provisions can still be removed before the Farm Bill moves forward.

This fight will determine who controls pesticide rules in America — communities or chemical companies.

Key Takeaways

The Farm Bill includes three provisions that could shield pesticide companies from lawsuits.

They could also strip states and towns of authority to regulate pesticide use locally.

Environmental protections tied to waterways and wildlife could be weakened.

The Pingree amendment would remove those provisions entirely and restore current law. @amtoxicology @chelliepingree

**May 7, 2025 (joint letter from House Oversight Chairman James Comer and two other Republican committee chairs sharing investigation findings with the DOJ).**

The House Oversight Committee (led by Rep. James Comer, R-Ky.), along with the House Judiciary Committee (led by Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio) and the Committee on House Administration (led by Rep. Bryan Steil, R-Wis.), sent a letter on that date to Attorney General Pam Bondi. **Context on timing and related actions**:
- The Oversight-led probe began earlier, with a September 20, 2024, letter requesting Treasury’s Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs) on potential fraud linked to ActBlue donations.
- Texas AG Ken Paxton issued his own separate criminal referral to the DOJ on October 24, 2024, citing straw donations and election law violations via ActBlue.
- The House committees released an interim staff report on fraud risks in early April 2025, issued subpoenas, and continued oversight into 2025.
- As of early 2026, Comer publicly expressed frustration that certain committee criminal referrals (including those tied to ActBlue findings) had seen limited DOJ follow-through under AG Bondi.

The May 7, 2025, joint letter is the documented instance matching the question. ActBlue has denied systemic issues, called the probes politically motivated, and pushed back on subpoenas.

Each week, we share stories of people whose lives leave a permanent imprint on our community. This week, we honor one of those rare individuals whose presence made our corner of the world better, stronger, and more connected: Art Younglove of Bristol Borough and Levittown, whom we sadly lost earlier this year after a courageous battle with cancer.

Art was a giant among men in every sense—kind, warm, generous, whip-smart, talented, and utterly one of a kind. But what stayed with you most was something even greater: he was a truly good man.

A proud United States Army veteran and Rohm and Haas employee for more than four decades, Art lived a life grounded in duty, humility, and service. But for so many across our community, he was known most of all as the steadfast Adjutant of Robert Bracken American Legion Post 382 and the heart and soul of the Bracken Cavaliers Drum and Bugle Corps.

If you grew up in Bucks County, as I did, chances are you saw them, heard them before you saw them, or maybe even marched alongside them. The Bracken legacy is not just part of our history—it is part of our identity. And Art was one of its great caretakers.

He carried that legacy forward with extraordinary pride and devotion, helping guide the Corps into its 100th year and playing a leading role in orchestrating its centennial celebration. He also helped bring to life the remarkable mural that now stands in Historic Bristol Borough in tribute to this special organization and all it has meant to generations of families in our community. Art understood something important: history does not live on through stone and paint alone. It lives on in the people who protect it, the traditions that bind us together, and the hometown pride that reminds us who we are.

Yesterday, Art would have turned 87 years old. So today, we gathered with his family and friends at the Bristol Borough Veterans Memorial—a place that meant so much to him—to honor a man who meant so much to so many.

Art was a patriot, steward of tradition, and builder of community,  who gave of himself quietly and generously, and in doing so helped preserve not only an institution, but a spirit of pride, belonging, and connection that will live on far beyond him.

Please join me in extending our deepest condolences to his wife, Grace; his children, Leeann, Catherine, and James; his sisters, Helen and Mary; and all who knew and loved him.

For his service to our nation, his devotion to our community, and the legacy he leaves behind, Art will always be remembered as a true Hometown Hero. 🇺🇸

In its 136-year history, the Perkasie Fire Company has lost only two firefighters in the line of duty, and last night, exactly 100 years later, we came together to remember them.

At the very moment that call came in on April 1, 1926, along with neighboring departments, we retraced the final route of Firefighters Jacob Crouthamel and Will Sames in an incredibly moving tribute. 

Working closely with our volunteer firefighters in Perkasie and across our community, I have seen firsthand the selfless service, tireless training, and deep love of neighbor this calling demands. These men and women do not simply respond to emergencies. They prepare constantly, sacrifice quietly, and stand ready at all hours to protect the people and places they love.

And last night was a powerful demonstration that while much has changed over the last hundred years, the courage and selflessness required to answer the call have not.

May we always remember Firefighters Jacob Crouthamel and Will Sames, and never stop honoring and supporting all our fire heroes who stand guard of our community.

En ambos casos se reportaron traslados fallidos hacia la prisión de Canaleta y devoluciones al centro de instrucción, una práctica que incrementa la presión psicológica y la incertidumbre sobre su situación.

⚠️ Los casos documentados muestran un patrón preocupante: detenciones diferidas; uso de cargos graves para castigar la protesta; prisión provisional como regla; restricciones al contacto familiar; falta de transparencia procesal; y exposición de menores a entornos incompatibles con su protección.

Oral arguments are underway at the Supreme Court in a case that could strip citizenship from children born on American soil.

The Constitution is unequivocal. The 14th Amendment guarantees birthright citizenship, and the Supreme Court has affirmed it for more than a century. President Donald Trump’s executive order terminating birthright citizenship blatantly violates the plain meaning of the Constitution and the Court’s own precedents.

And now he is showing up at the Supreme Court itself, an unmistakable attempt to pressure and intimidate the justices as they weigh a fundamental question of constitutional law.

What is at stake is nothing less than the rule of law itself. An effort to rewrite the Constitution by executive fiat, backed by political pressure on the Court, would sow chaos in the lives of millions and erode the judiciary’s role as a check on executive overreach.

It would also fundamentally undermine what it means to be an American. Birthright citizenship is not a technicality, it is a defining promise of this country: that anyone born here belongs here. To strip that away is to redraw the boundaries of American identity itself.

On this day in 1923, Colonel Joe Madison Jackson, an American hero, was born in Newnan, Georgia.

After graduating from Newnan High School, Joe enlisted in the U.S. Army Air Corps, the predecessor of the U.S. Air Force.

Eventually earning the rank of Colonel, Joe Jackson served with distinction in World War II, the Korean War, and the Vietnam War. 

During the Battle of Kham Duc of the Vietnam War in 1968, Colonel Jackson demonstrated extraordinary courage by flying his aircraft through intense enemy fire to rescue three stranded servicemen.  For his bravery during that mission, Colonel Jackson was presented the Medal of Honor by President Lyndon B. Johnson on January 16, 1969. 

Colonel Jackson retired from the U.S. Air Force in 1974 after more than 33 years of honorable service to our Country.

Colonel Jackson will forever be remembered as one of the greatest Americans from Georgia’s 3rd Congressional District!

This morning I received a behind-the-scenes tour of the OVEC-IKEC Kyger Creek Station. Kyger has five 217 megawatt generating units that have a total capacity of 1,085 megawatts. This station, along with Clifty Creek Station, were the largest power plants ever built by a private industry.

Situated along the Ohio River at Cheshire, Ohio, Kyger Creek Station was originally built to provide electric power to the Atomic Energy Commission's (Department of Energy) gaseous diffusion plant in Piketon, Ohio. Since 2003, the power produced by Kyger Creek Station has been supplied to companies and customers, with the plant generating over 4.8 million megawatts of power in 2024. 

It was wonderful to see exactly how this plant operates and talk with leadership about the critical role it plays in providing local jobs in our community and securing our energy supply. In Congress, I will continue pushing to unleash American energy and back our critical local industries. Thank you to the Kyger team for the tour!
